opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of what people experience as a step change is really the accumulation of many smaller, fairly continuous improvements that happen to cross a threshold of usefulness all at once. If you look at the underlying metrics, things like loss on held-out data or performance across a broad suite of evals, progress tends to look surprisingly smooth. But the way a person interacts with a model isn't smooth. You either trust it to do the task or you don't. You either hand it the whole coding problem or you keep it on a short leash.

So when a model gets a bit more reliable at long chains of reasoning, a bit better at catching its own mistakes, a bit better at following an instruction from twenty turns ago, each of those might be a modest gain on paper. Multiply them together over a long task, though, and the probability of getting all the way to a correct answer can jump dramatically. That's where the feeling of a qualitative leap comes from: the compounding of reliability.

There's also a real sense in which some of the recent jumps are more genuine discontinuities in method rather than just scale. Training models to think for longer before answering, and using reinforcement learning to make that thinking actually productive, opened up a new axis to push on. Previously the main lever was pretraining compute. Now you have test-time compute and post-training as additional levers, and when a new lever gets pulled hard for the first time you often see a bigger visible gain than you'd expect from the trend line.

And then, honestly, part of it is perception. People tend to probe models with the tasks that previous models failed at. So the moment of release is when you're most likely to notice the new things it can do, and the "wow" moments get amplified. A few months later that becomes the new baseline, and people start noticing the failure modes again. I think holding both views at once is useful: the progress is real and often quite fast, but it's usually more continuous underneath than the release-day experience suggests.

r001.rationale: The response says small reliability gains can compound over a long task, but it does not contrast uncertainty about individual training changes with predictability of accumulated improvements.

r002.rationale: It explains that gradual improvements can cross a threshold of usefulness, making the change feel sudden to users.

r003.rationale: It says release time is when people are most likely to notice new capabilities, contributing to the impression of a step change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because from the outside it looks like these discontinuous jumps, and from the inside it really doesn't feel that way. When you're on the team, you're watching a fairly smooth curve. Loss goes down, evals tick up a point or two at a time, and there's rarely a single day where everyone gasps.

So I think there are a few things going on. The first is that the underlying capability is improving continuously, but the way we measure it, and the way people experience it, is thresholded. A model that gets a multi-step math problem right 30 percent of the time feels broken. A model that gets it right 90 percent of the time feels like a different kind of entity, even though the gap in log-likelihood or whatever the underlying quantity is may be fairly modest. Reliability crossing some usability bar is what people perceive as a step change. There's a nice framing of this where you think of a task as requiring a chain of steps, and if your per-step accuracy goes from 95 to 99 percent, the chance of completing a twenty-step chain goes from about a third to about four-fifths. Small smooth change underneath, big phase-transition-looking change on top.

The second thing is that releases bundle a lot of changes. A new model isn't one intervention. It's more compute, better data, a bunch of architectural and training tweaks, and usually a lot of post-training work that teaches the model how to actually use capabilities it already latently had. Each of those is incremental, but you ship them all at once with a version number on them, so the public sees a sawtooth even though the research process was closer to a ramp.

And then the third piece, which I find most interesting, is that some capabilities genuinely do look emergent at the level of individual tasks, even if aggregate metrics are smooth. You'll see a benchmark sit near chance for a long time and then move quickly. A lot of that turns out to be an artifact of how you score it, exact-match versus partial credit, that sort of thing. But I don't think it's entirely an artifact. Models seem to pick up certain compositional abilities, like chaining together reasoning or reliably following a long structured format, in a way where the representations have to get to a certain quality before the behaviour becomes useful at all.

So my honest answer is that the step changes are mostly real to the user and mostly not real to the scaling curve. Both of those are true at once, and I think a lot of the confusion in the discourse comes from people arguing about one while looking at the other.

r001.rationale: The response says releases bundle incremental changes and describes a smooth overall curve, but it does not contrast uncertainty about the benefit of individual changes with predictability of accumulated improvements.

r002.rationale: It explains that capability improves continuously while usability thresholds make models feel qualitatively different once reliability crosses a bar.

r003.rationale: It says many incremental changes are bundled into a new model and shipped together under a version number, creating a sawtooth impression for the public.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things going on. One is that the underlying models are improving fairly smoothly. As you put more compute into training, you tend to see predictable improvements in how well they model language. But that doesn’t necessarily translate into a smooth experience for someone using the system.

If a task requires several things to go right, a small improvement in each of those can make a big difference to whether the whole task succeeds. You can go from a model that occasionally does something impressive but needs constant supervision to one that works reliably enough to be useful. That feels like a step change, even if the underlying improvement was gradual.

The other thing is that people encounter these models through discrete releases. They don’t see every intermediate checkpoint. So there’s a continuous process behind the scenes, and then a new release arrives and suddenly a whole set of things seems possible.

That doesn’t rule out more genuinely abrupt changes in particular capabilities. But I’d be cautious about taking a striking jump on a benchmark, or in someone’s experience, as evidence that the underlying learning process itself had a discontinuity.

r001.rationale: The response says capability improvements from more compute tend to be predictable, but does not contrast that with uncertainty about the benefit of individual training changes.

r002.rationale: It explains that small improvements can make a task reliably successful, turning occasional impressive results into something useful and making the change feel abrupt.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says people encounter models through discrete releases and do not see the intermediate checkpoints, which makes continuous progress appear sudden.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things going on. One is that the underlying improvements can be quite smooth, while our experience of them is much less smooth. If a model gets steadily better at each part of a task, there can be a point where it suddenly becomes reliable enough to do the whole thing. From the user’s perspective, that feels like a new capability, even though the ingredients were improving gradually.

The other is that people encounter models as discrete releases. You don’t necessarily see all the intermediate checkpoints, so a continuous improvement in training can look like a jump when the next model becomes available.

That doesn’t mean every apparent step change is just an artifact. But I’d distinguish a jump in a benchmark score, a jump in how useful the model feels, and a genuinely abrupt change in the underlying capability. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts smooth underlying improvement with a less smooth user experience, but does not discuss uncertainty about individual training changes or predictability of accumulated gains.

r002.rationale: It explains that gradual improvements can cross a reliability threshold, making a capability feel suddenly new to users.

r003.rationale: It says people encounter discrete releases without seeing intermediate checkpoints, so continuous improvement can look like a jump.
